questions.stem: What colour change shows that acidified dichromate has oxidised an alcohol?

options.text: Orange to green, as Cr2O7 2- is reduced to Cr3+
options.explanation: The oxidising agent turns from orange dichromate to green chromium(III) as it works.

options.text: Green to orange, as the chromium gains electrons
options.explanation: The change runs the other way; oxidation of the alcohol reduces the chromium.

options.text: Colourless to pink
options.explanation: That describes an indicator, not dichromate.

options.text: No colour change ever occurs
options.explanation: The orange-to-green shift is the standard observable.

questions.stem: Why must potassium dichromate be acidified to act as an oxidising agent?

options.text: Acid prevents the alcohol from evaporating
options.explanation: Acidification has nothing to do with volatility.

options.text: Its reduction requires hydrogen ions, which the dilute acid supplies
options.explanation: The Cr2O7 2- to Cr3+ reduction consumes H+, so the acidic medium is a chemical requirement.

options.text: The acid makes the solution orange so the colour change is visible
options.explanation: Dichromate is orange before acidification plays any role.

options.text: The acid catalyses the alcohol's dehydration instead
options.explanation: The acid enables the dichromate's own reduction, not dehydration.

questions.stem: Oxidising a secondary alcohol with acidified dichromate produces

options.text: A carboxylic acid after prolonged reflux
options.explanation: Acids come from oxidising aldehydes of primary alcohols.

options.text: No reaction at all
options.explanation: Only tertiary alcohols fail to oxidise.

options.text: A ketone, which resists further oxidation
options.explanation: Secondary alcohols stop at the ketone stage.

options.text: An aldehyde that must be distilled off quickly
options.explanation: Aldehydes come from primary alcohols.

questions.stem: Why can the aldehyde be separated from the reaction mixture as it forms?

options.text: It is denser than the oxidising agent and sinks
options.explanation: Density is irrelevant; volatility does the separating.

options.text: It is insoluble in all solvents and precipitates
options.explanation: The aldehyde is a liquid product, not a precipitate.

options.text: It reacts with the condenser water irreversibly
options.explanation: The condenser merely condenses vapour back or out.

options.text: Its boiling point is lower than the alcohol's, so it distils out before further oxidation
options.explanation: Removing the aldehyde by its lower boiling point halts the oxidation at the aldehyde stage.

questions.stem: If the aldehyde is not distilled off and refluxing continues with excess oxidising agent, the product becomes

options.text: The carboxylic acid, the fully oxidised product
options.explanation: Extended reflux with excess dichromate drives primary alcohols all the way to the acid.

options.text: The ketone, by rearrangement
options.explanation: Ketones come from secondary alcohols; no rearrangement occurs here.

options.text: Back to the alcohol, by reduction
options.explanation: The oxidising agent cannot reduce anything; the direction is uphill only.

options.text: An ester, by condensation
options.explanation: Esterification needs an acid plus alcohol set-up, not this oxidation.

questions.stem: State the oxidation products for primary, secondary and tertiary alcohols with acidified dichromate.
questions.modelAnswer: Primary alcohols give aldehydes then carboxylic acids, secondary alcohols give ketones only, and tertiary alcohols do not oxidise.

questions.stem: State what acidified means in the context of potassium dichromate(VI).
questions.modelAnswer: The dichromate is dissolved in dilute acid, typically dilute sulfuric acid, which supplies the hydrogen ions its reduction needs.

questions.stem: Explain why the dichromate ions are reduced while the alcohol is oxidised.
questions.modelAnswer: Oxidation and reduction happen together: the alcohol loses hydrogen and electrons, and those electrons reduce the orange dichromate to green chromium(III), so the reagent's colour change is the mirror of the alcohol's oxidation.

questions.stem: A mixture of propan-1-ol and propan-2-ol is oxidised with excess acidified dichromate under reflux. State the organic products and the colour change observed.
questions.modelAnswer: Propanoic acid from the primary alcohol and propanone from the secondary alcohol form, and the reagent turns from orange to green as the dichromate is reduced to chromium(III).

questions.stem: What is observed when Fehling's solution is warmed with an aldehyde?

options.text: Effervescence of carbon dioxide
options.explanation: No gas is released in the Fehling's test.

options.text: The clear blue solution turns opaque and a red precipitate of copper(I) oxide forms
options.explanation: Reduced Cu+ precipitates as red Cu2O, clouding the blue solution.

options.text: A silver mirror forms on the tube wall
options.explanation: That is Tollens' positive result, not Fehling's.

options.text: The solution turns bright green
options.explanation: Green belongs to dichromate reduction.

questions.stem: Tollens' reagent is described as ammoniacal silver nitrate because it is

options.text: Ammonia gas bubbled through a copper salt
options.explanation: Copper belongs to Fehling's solution.

options.text: Silver metal suspended in nitric acid
options.explanation: The reagent carries dissolved Ag+ ions, not metal powder in acid.

options.text: Silver nitrate dissolved in water with ammonia in excess, alkaline throughout
options.explanation: The ammonia supplies the alkaline medium that keeps silver ions available.

options.text: Solid silver nitrate dissolved in alcohol
options.explanation: Tollens' reagent is aqueous and alkaline, not alcoholic.

questions.stem: Why do ketones give negative results with both Fehling's and Tollens' reagents?

options.text: Ketones reduce the reagents too fast to observe
options.explanation: Fast reduction would give a positive test, the opposite of observed.

options.text: Ketones are insoluble in alkaline solution
options.explanation: Solubility is not the deciding factor; oxidisability is.

options.text: The reagents only test for alcohols
options.explanation: The reagents specifically detect the oxidisable aldehyde group.

options.text: Ketones cannot be oxidised to carboxylic acids by these mild agents, so the metal ions stay unreduced
options.explanation: No oxidation means no reduction of Cu2+ or Ag+, hence no colour change or mirror.

questions.stem: In alkaline conditions the carboxylic acid formed from an aldehyde exists as

options.text: A carboxylate ion, often paired as a sodium salt
options.explanation: Alkali removes the acid proton, giving -COO- that pairs with metal ions.

options.text: The neutral -COOH acid throughout
options.explanation: Alkaline conditions deprotonate the acid immediately.

options.text: An aldehyde again by hydrolysis
options.explanation: Nothing hydrolyses back to the aldehyde here.

options.text: An ester with the solvent
options.explanation: No esterification occurs in the alkaline test medium.

questions.stem: Which metal ion is reduced when Tollens' reagent reacts positively?

options.text: Nitrate ion, reduced to nitrogen dioxide
options.explanation: The nitrate is a spectator; silver is the working ion.

options.text: Silver ion, Ag+, reduced to metallic silver atoms
options.explanation: The Ag+ ions gain electrons and plate out as the silver mirror.

options.text: Copper(II) ion, reduced to copper(I) oxide
options.explanation: That is Fehling's solution chemistry.

options.text: Ammonium ion, reduced to ammonia
options.explanation: Ammonia is already the medium, not the reduced species.

questions.stem: State the positive observations for Fehling's and Tollens' tests.
questions.modelAnswer: Fehling's gives an opaque red precipitate of copper(I) oxide; Tollens' gives a silver mirror on the tube.

questions.stem: Name the oxidising species in Fehling's solution.
questions.modelAnswer: Copper(II) ions in alkaline solution are the oxidising agent that reduces to Cu+ in the red oxide precipitate.

questions.stem: Explain why the Tollens' test deposits silver on the glass rather than forming a precipitate.
questions.modelAnswer: The reduced silver atoms are uncharged metal that adheres to the clean glass surface as a reflective film instead of clustering into an insoluble ionic solid, which is why the tube mirrors rather than clouds.

questions.stem: Two unlabelled liquids are propanal and propanone. Describe how one test distinguishes them, stating the reagent and both possible outcomes.
questions.modelAnswer: Warm each with Tollens' reagent: propanal gives the silver mirror within minutes while propanone leaves the reagent clear, so the mirror identifies the aldehyde and the unchanged tube the ketone.

questions.stem: Which technique produces a carboxylic acid from a primary alcohol?

options.text: Shaking with sodium carbonate solution
options.explanation: That is a washing step, not an oxidation.

options.text: Drying over anhydrous sulfate
options.explanation: Drying removes water; it performs no oxidation.

options.text: Heating under reflux with excess oxidising agent
options.explanation: Retention in the flask drives oxidation all the way to the acid.

options.text: Distillation with addition of the alcohol
options.explanation: That technique deliberately stops at the aldehyde.

questions.stem: In distillation with addition, the alcohol is added slowly to the heated oxidising agent because

options.text: The alcohol must be conserved because it is expensive
options.explanation: Economy is not the chemical reason; the volatile product's escape is.

options.text: Adding fast would freeze the oxidising agent
options.explanation: Nothing freezes; the reason is product protection.

options.text: The oxidising agent reacts violently with all alcohols
options.explanation: Controlled addition protects the aldehyde from over-oxidation, not the apparatus from violence.

options.text: Each drop oxidises promptly and its aldehyde distils away before further oxidation
options.explanation: Slow feeding keeps the aldehyde's residence time in the oxidant as short as possible.

questions.stem: What keeps the products inside the flask during heating under reflux?

options.text: The vertical condenser condenses escaping vapour and returns it to the mixture
options.explanation: Vapours hit the cold jacket glass and drip back, so nothing is lost while heating continues.

options.text: A sealed stopper blocks the flask neck
options.explanation: Reflux flasks are open at the top to the condenser, not sealed.

options.text: The reaction temperature stays below every boiling point
options.explanation: Reflux involves boiling; retention is mechanical, not thermal.

options.text: The products are non-volatile solids
options.explanation: The products are volatile liquids deliberately retained.

questions.stem: Why does the aldehyde leave the reaction zone immediately in distillation with addition?

options.text: The condenser water pushes it out of the flask
options.explanation: The condenser sits outside the flask; pressure of water plays no role.

options.text: Its boiling point is much lower than the alcohol's, so it vapourises as soon as it forms
options.explanation: The boiling-point gap makes the aldehyde the first volatile species to leave the hot mixture.

options.text: It is repelled by the oxidising agent chemically
options.explanation: No repulsion exists; volatility alone drives the escape.

options.text: It is insoluble in the oxidising solution and floats out
options.explanation: Immiscibility is not the escape route; vapourisation is.

questions.stem: Oxidising a secondary alcohol under reflux gives which outcome?

options.text: The carboxylic acid
options.explanation: Acids arise from primary alcohols only.

options.text: No oxidation, since reflux blocks secondary alcohols
options.explanation: Secondary alcohols oxidise readily under reflux to ketones.

options.text: The ketone, the ceiling product for secondary alcohols
options.explanation: Reflux with excess oxidant delivers the ketone, which cannot oxidise further.

options.text: A mixture of aldehyde and ketone
options.explanation: Secondary alcohols never pass through aldehydes.

questions.stem: State which apparatus choice suits full oxidation and which suits stopping at the aldehyde.
questions.modelAnswer: Reflux suits full oxidation to acids or ketones, and distillation with addition suits collecting the aldehyde before over-oxidation.

questions.stem: Describe how the alcohol is introduced in the distillation-with-addition technique.
questions.modelAnswer: The oxidant alone sits on the heat while the alcohol drips in slowly, drop by drop, so each portion oxidises and its aldehyde distils away at once.

questions.stem: Explain why reflux cannot be used when the aldehyde is the target product.
questions.modelAnswer: Reflux retains every volatile species in contact with the oxidant, so any aldehyde formed would be re-oxidised to the acid; the target requires its immediate removal, which only distillation provides.

questions.stem: A student wants propanal from propan-1-ol but sets up reflux by mistake. State the product obtained after full reflux with excess oxidant and the apparatus that should have been used.
questions.modelAnswer: Propanoic acid, since retained aldehyde is oxidised further under reflux; the correct set-up was distillation with addition, dripping the alcohol into heated oxidant and collecting the distilled propanal.
